paras: The lynching of Thomas James Noakes took place early on August 7, 1881, when masked and armed men took him from the jail at Oroville, Butte County, California, and hanged him from an oak tree on the road to Chico. Noakes was being held for the killing of A. J. Crum at Chico about three weeks earlier. A coroner's jury found that he died by mob violence and named no one, and the case drew opposing editorials in California and Nevada papers.

According to the Oroville correspondent of the Sacramento Daily Record-Union, Noakes, a powerful man over six feet tall, had knocked Crum down with his fist and then kicked and beaten him to death. The same dispatch described Crum as a small man over fifty and a cripple who did not know Noakes, and said the only provocation Noakes alleged was a remark about his brother, which Crum denied. No paper stated Noakes's race; the inquest described him as about 40 and believed to be a native of Missouri.

With the under sheriff ill, jailer Knowles was alone at the jail when a knock came at about 2 a.m. and a voice claimed to be an officer from Biggs with a prisoner. When he opened the door, about fifteen masked and armed men pushed in, disarmed him and demanded the keys, which he refused to give up. Using tools they had brought, the men forced two wooden and two iron doors to reach the iron tank where Noakes was held, and he surrendered without resistance.

They tied his hands, put him in a waiting wagon under guard and drove across the river toward Chico, while guards they had posted watched the streets around the court-house. A man coming into town met the party on the road and judged that there were forty or more in it. At Crum's old place, about ten miles from Oroville, Noakes was hanged from the limb of a large oak, his hands tied behind him and his feet bound. Sheriff Sprague, returning from a trip to Durham, found the body still hanging early that morning.

Coroner Mitchell had the body brought to town, and on August 8 his jury found that Noakes died 'by being hanged by mob violence', while the verdict was silent on who took part. The body bore no marks of violence except those of the rope. None of the men were known, the Oroville correspondent wrote, and no one seemed to want to know them. No report of arrests, a grand jury inquiry or a trial appears in the coverage.

The Record-Union printed its Oroville dispatch under the heading 'Judge Lynch in Butte County—A Murderer Taken from Jail by Citizens and Hanged', calling Noakes a murderer outright. A shorter San Francisco wire dispatch ran on August 8 in the New-York Tribune as 'Lynch Law in California' and in the Chicago Tribune as 'Hanged by a Mob'. News-summary columns in Wilmington, Washington, Lancaster and Savannah carried the same item, often with misprinted initials or place names such as 'Oreville' and 'Orville'. The inquest followed on August 9 in papers such as the Eureka Daily Sentinel, which headed it 'Noakes Hanged by Vigilantes', and the New-York Tribune, which used 'A Mob as a Hangman'.

The Record-Union's own editorial declared that 'A lynching is not an execution; it is a murder', and put journals that excused such outrages next in guilt to the lynchers. The Carson City Morning Appeal, repeating the Oroville correspondent's description almost word for word, called lynching horrible but said lax courts had made it 'a necessity of the times' and that Noakes was better dangling from the oak than freed on a technicality. The Weekly Elko Independent called Noakes a 'cowardly brute' who was 'treated just as he deserved'.

Weeks later the German-language Hermanner Volksblatt of Missouri, which called the hanging 'Volksjustiz' [popular justice], put the band at 20 to 25 mounted men said to be citizens of Chico and the hanging at Caine's Ranch, about halfway to Chico. The wire dispatch placed the tree only 'a short distance from the town', while the local Oroville correspondent, the most detailed source, put it about ten miles out.

reader.title: Lynching of Thomas James Noakes
chips: Lynching of any race (not in the anti-Black count)
bases: Masked, armed men broke into the Butte County jail at Oroville, took the prisoner Noakes out and hanged him from a tree on the Chico road (A1, A4, A33).

About fifteen masked men (forty or more by one roadside estimate, 20 to 25 in another account) seized Noakes from jail without any legal authority and hanged him for the killing of A. J. Crum, of which he stood accused (A1, A33); the coroner's jury found he died 'by being hanged by mob violence' (A12).

The Sacramento Record-Union's Oroville correspondent (A1), the San Francisco wire dispatch (A4, A8), the coroner's verdict (A12, A15) and a separately written German account (A33) agree on the seizure from jail and the hanging.

accounts.gist: About fifteen masked men posing as an officer from Biggs with a prisoner seized the jailer, forced their way to Noakes's cell, drove him toward Chico and hanged him at Crum's old place; nobody knew or wanted to know who they were.

accounts.label: Wire report (San Francisco)
accounts.gist: Masked and armed men took Noakes from jail, carried him a short distance from town and hanged him to a tree; he had killed Crum by kicking him.

accounts.label: Coroner's jury
accounts.gist: Thomas James Noakes died on the morning of August 7 by hanging by mob violence; the verdict named no one.

accounts.label: German-language account (Hermanner Volksblatt)
accounts.gist: 20 to 25 masked, mounted men, said to be Chico citizens, broke the cell door after the deputy refused the keys and hanged Noakes from an oak at Caine's Ranch before dawn, then rode back to Chico.

framing.detail: The Sacramento Record-Union's dispatch headlined 'Judge Lynch in Butte County—A Murderer Taken from Jail by Citizens and Hanged' and stressed the brutality of Crum's killing and local approval.
The Record-Union editorial 'The Oroville Lynching' called the lynching a murder and blamed journals that excuse such outrages.
The Carson City Morning Appeal called lynching horrible but said lax courts had made lynch law 'a necessity of the times'.
The Weekly Elko Independent called Noakes a 'cowardly brute' who was 'treated just as he deserved'.
Eastern and Southern papers ran the San Francisco dispatch in news summaries under heads such as 'Lynch Law in California' and 'Hanged by a Mob'.
